17 A rock of mass 40 kg is released from rest from a height of 20 m above the surface of a planet.
The rock has a kinetic energy of 32 kJ when it hits the surface of the planet. The planet does not
have an atmosphere.
What is the weight of the rock on the surface of the planet?
A
1.6 N
B
390 N
C
1.6 kN
D
64 kN

hints: Notice the rock falls 20 m with no atmosphere, so the 32 kJ of kinetic energy at impact must have come entirely from loss of gravitational potential energy.
Recall $loss$ $in$ $GPE = mgh$ with $m = 40 \text{ kg}$, $h = 20 \text{ m}$ and $32 \text{ kJ} = 32000 \text{ J}$, which lets you find the planet's $g$.
Connect weight to $W = mg$ using the same mass of 40 kg and the $g$ you found from the energy change, then check N against kN.
walkthrough: Identify the energy transfer: released from rest with no air resistance, so loss in gravitational potential energy equals gain in kinetic energy.
Write $mgh = KE$ with $m = 40 \text{ kg}$, $h = 20 \text{ m}$ and $KE = 32 \text{ kJ} = 32000 \text{ J}$.
Solve for the field strength: $g = 32000/800 = 40 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Calculate weight on the surface: $W = mg = 40 \times 40 = 1600 \text{ N} = 1.6 \text{ kN}$.

A.explanation: 1.6 N is 1000 times too small and comes from missing the kJ to J conversion for the 32 kJ kinetic energy.

B.explanation: 390 N is close to the Earth weight $40 \times 9.81$, but the 32 kJ fall over 20 m shows the gravitational field here is much stronger.

C.explanation: Loss of potential energy $mgh$ equals the 32000 J gain in kinetic energy, giving $g = 40 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and weight $mg = 1600 \text{ N}$.

D.explanation: 64 kN multiplies mass by energy or misuses $mgh$, giving a value 40 times too large with incorrect units.
